classes.label: Apple_fruit_healthy
classes.cause: No disease signs detected.
actions: Keep scouting on your normal schedule.
Avoid overhead watering late in the day.

classes.label: Apple_fruit_visible_damage
classes.cause: Visible fruit damage is present, but one photo cannot separate infection from bruising, sun injury, insect feeding, or storage damage.
actions: Inspect several fruit and photograph the damaged area in sharp daylight.
Remove badly rotted fruit and sanitize harvest or storage surfaces.
Confirm the cause before applying any pesticide; visible damage alone is not a spray recommendation.

classes.label: Apple_leaf_alternaria_leaf_blotch
classes.cause: Foliar blotch pathogen. Irregular merging lesions.
actions: Remove affected leaves and debris.
Protectant fungicide during wet periods.
Improve airflow; rotate.

classes.label: Apple_leaf_apple_mosaic_virus
classes.cause: Plant virus. No cure; spread mechanically and by insect vectors.
actions: Remove and destroy infected plants -- they are a reservoir.
Disinfect hands and tools between plants.
Use resistant varieties and control insect vectors.

classes.label: Apple_leaf_apple_scab
classes.cause: Scab fungus. Corky or olive-brown lesions on leaves and fruit.
actions: Clear fallen leaves to break the overwintering cycle.
Protectant fungicide during the early-season infection window.
Resistant cultivars when replanting.

classes.label: Apple_leaf_black_rot
classes.cause: Rot pathogen. Tissue breakdown, often starting at wounds or in wet conditions.
actions: Remove and destroy affected tissue and fallen fruit.
Improve drainage and airflow; avoid injuring plants.
Protectant fungicide where an approved product exists.

classes.label: Apple_leaf_cedar_apple_rust
classes.cause: Rust fungus. Orange to brown pustules that release spores when rubbed.
actions: Remove badly infected leaves; clear debris at end of season.
Fungicide if it reaches the upper canopy early.
Resistant varieties and wider spacing reduce recurrence.

classes.label: Cucumber_fruit_pythium_fruit_rot

Protectant fungicide where an approved product exists.

classes.label: Cucumber_leaf_anthracnose
classes.cause: Anthracnose fungus. Sunken dark lesions on leaves, stems and fruit; splash-spread.
actions: Remove infected tissue and fallen debris.
Protectant fungicide through wet weather.
Improve drainage and airflow; avoid overhead watering.

classes.label: Cucumber_leaf_bacterial_wilt
classes.cause: Bacterial wilt, usually vectored by cucumber beetles. Plants wilt with no recovery overnight.
actions: Remove wilting plants immediately -- they infect the beetles that move on.

classes.label: Cucumber_leaf_downy_mildew
classes.cause: Oomycete downy mildew. Needs leaf wetness; spreads fast in cool humid weather.
actions: Stop overhead watering and improve airflow immediately.
Apply an oomycete-active fungicide -- powdery mildew products do not work on downy mildew.
Remove and destroy infected foliage; rotate next season.

classes.label: Cucumber_leaf_gummy_stem_blight
classes.cause: Gummy stem blight (Didymella/​Stagonosporopsis). It survives on seed and crop debris and spreads in wet canopies.
actions: Remove infected vines and cucurbit debris; do not save seed from affected plants.
Use drip irrigation and open the canopy so foliage dries quickly.
Confirm locally before treatment and rotate fungicide modes of action if spraying is justified.

classes.label: Lemon_fruit_citrus_canker

actions: Check local rules -- citrus canker is notifiable in many regions.
Remove and destroy infected material; disinfect tools between trees.
Copper protectant and windbreaks to limit wind-driven spread.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_melanose
classes.cause: Citrus melanose fungus. Inoculum comes mainly from dead twigs during wet weather.
actions: Prune dead twigs and open the canopy before the rainy infection period.
Improve airflow and avoid prolonged overhead irrigation.
Use a locally approved protectant only when crop stage and wet-weather risk justify it.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_mite_damage
classes.cause: Likely mite feeding damage. Mites build fastest in hot, dusty conditions and broad-spectrum insecticides can worsen outbreaks by killing predators.

Reduce dust and water stress, wash small plants, and conserve predatory mites.
If thresholds justify treatment, use a locally approved selective miticide or horticultural oil and cover leaf undersides.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_nutrient_deficiency
classes.cause: Possible discoloration pattern resembling examples labelled nutrient deficiency. A photo cannot confirm a nutrient shortage, identify a missing nutrient, or rule out another cause.
actions: Photograph affected and unaffected leaves from the same plant and note their positions.
Record recent watering and fertilizer changes without changing the application rate based on this result.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_spider_mite

Reduce dust and water stress; conserve or release predatory mites where practical.
Use soap, horticultural oil, or a selective locally approved miticide only when scouting pressure justifies it.

classes.label: Tomato_leaf_tomato_mosaic_virus
classes.cause: Plant virus. No cure; spread mechanically and by insect vectors.
actions: Remove and destroy infected plants -- they are a reservoir.
Disinfect hands and tools between plants.
Use resistant varieties and control insect vectors.

classes.label: Tomato_leaf_two_spotted_spider_mite
classes.diagnosis: Tomato leaf: two spotted spider mite
classes.cause: Spider-mite feeding causes fine stippling, bronzing, and sometimes webbing on leaf undersides.
actions: Confirm moving mites and eggs with a hand lens and map the infested area.
Reduce dust and water stress; conserve or release predatory mites where practical.
Use soap, horticultural oil, or a selective locally approved miticide only when scouting pressure justifies it.

classes.label: Tomato_leaf_yellow_leaf_curl_virus
classes.diagnosis: Tomato leaf: yellow leaf curl virus
classes.cause: Plant virus. No cure once a plant is infected.
actions: Rogue out infected plants promptly.
Control the insect vector -- that is what stops spread.
Plant certified stock and resistant varieties next season.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_algal_leaf_spot
classes.cause: Parasitic alga (Cephaleuros virescens). Raised orange or grey-green velvety patches, favoured by long leaf wetness and crowded, shaded canopies.
actions: Prune for light and airflow so leaves dry faster after rain or irrigation.
Remove badly spotted leaves and twigs; do not leave them under the tree.
Copper sprays help on severe trees, but fix the canopy and drainage first.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_anthracnose
classes.cause: Anthracnose fungus. Sunken dark lesions on leaves, stems and fruit; splash-spread.
actions: Remove infected tissue and fallen debris.
Protectant fungicide through wet weather.
Improve drainage and airflow; avoid overhead watering.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_bacterial_blight
classes.cause: Bacterial blight. Splashing water and contaminated tools commonly move it between plants.
actions: Avoid working wet plants and sanitize tools between blocks.
Remove severely affected tissue and use clean planting material.
Use copper only as a locally approved preventive; it will not cure existing lesions.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_bacterial_spot
classes.cause: Possible spotted-leaf pattern. The training label says 'bacterial spot', but a matching appearance does not confirm bacteria or identify a pathogen.
actions: Photograph both leaf surfaces and the wider plant while leaving the tissue in place.
Record how many plants show the pattern and whether it changes between scouting visits.
Ask a local agricultural extension specialist to confirm the cause and advise whether testing is needed before any treatment decision.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_black_spot
classes.cause: Dark spotting can have fungal, bacterial, or abiotic causes; crop and lesion details are needed to separate them.
actions: Photograph both leaf surfaces and any fruit symptoms for confirmation.
Remove fallen infected material and reduce leaf wetness.
Confirm the diagnosis with a crop specialist before applying a pesticide.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_citrus_canker
classes.cause: Bacterial canker. Raised corky lesions; regulated in many citrus regions.
actions: Check local rules -- citrus canker is notifiable in many regions.
Remove and destroy infected material; disinfect tools between trees.
Copper protectant and windbreaks to limit wind-driven spread.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_citrus_scab
classes.cause: Scab fungus. Corky or olive-brown lesions on leaves and fruit.
actions: Clear fallen leaves to break the overwintering cycle.
Protectant fungicide during the early-season infection window.
Resistant cultivars when replanting.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_curl_virus
classes.cause: Possible curled-leaf pattern. The training label includes 'virus', but this photo match does not establish a viral infection or its cause.
actions: Photograph both leaf surfaces and the whole plant while keeping the leaves attached.
Compare affected and unaffected leaves and record when the curling first appeared.
Ask a local agricultural extension specialist to confirm the cause before treatment; keep the plant intact while arranging that review.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_dry_or_senescent_leaf
classes.diagnosis: Lemon leaf: dry or senescent leaf
classes.cause: Possible dry-looking or aging-leaf pattern. This photo match does not establish whether the tissue is senescent or damaged, or why its appearance changed.
actions: Photograph the leaf and the whole plant, including unaffected leaves, without cutting tissue.
Record when the change appeared and check the watering record and visible condition of the planting area.
Arrange an agricultural extension review if the change is spreading or remains unexplained; confirm the cause before treatment.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_greening_HLB
classes.cause: Citrus greening (Huanglongbing), spread by psyllids. Incurable and fatal.
actions: There is no cure; infected trees are a source of spread.
Report it -- notifiable in many regions.
Remove infected trees, control psyllids, plant certified stock.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_healthy
classes.cause: No disease signs detected.
actions: Keep scouting on your normal schedule.
Avoid overhead watering late in the day.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_leaf_curl_unknown_cause
classes.diagnosis: Lemon leaf: leaf curl unknown cause
classes.cause: Leaf curling is visible, but an image alone cannot separate mites, sap-feeding insects, virus, herbicide drift, or water/root stress.
actions: Inspect both leaf surfaces with a hand lens for mites, insects, webbing, or mines.
Compare the pattern across the block and check irrigation, roots, and recent spray drift.
Isolate strongly affected nursery plants and confirm the cause before choosing any pesticide.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_leaf_spot_unspecified
classes.cause: Possible leaf-spot pattern with no established cause. This class is a visual symptom category and does not identify a pathogen or confirm an infectious disease.
actions: Take sharp photos of both leaf surfaces and a wider view of the plant.
Compare several affected and unaffected leaves and record whether the spots change over time.
Share those observations with a local agricultural extension specialist for confirmation before any treatment decision.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_leafminer
classes.cause: Leafminer larvae feeding between the upper and lower leaf surfaces.
actions: Remove a small number of mined leaves and conserve parasitoid wasps.
Use yellow sticky cards to track adult pressure rather than spraying by calendar.
Treat only when scouting thresholds justify it; broad-spectrum insecticides can kill beneficials.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_melanose
classes.cause: Citrus melanose fungus. Inoculum comes mainly from dead twigs during wet weather.
actions: Prune dead twigs and open the canopy before the rainy infection period.
Improve airflow and avoid prolonged overhead irrigation.
Use a locally approved protectant only when crop stage and wet-weather risk justify it.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_mite_damage
classes.cause: Likely mite feeding damage. Mites build fastest in hot, dusty conditions and broad-spectrum insecticides can worsen outbreaks by killing predators.
actions: Confirm mites or eggs on leaf undersides with a hand lens before treating.
Reduce dust and water stress, wash small plants, and conserve predatory mites.
If thresholds justify treatment, use a locally approved selective miticide or horticultural oil and cover leaf undersides.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_nutrient_deficiency
classes.cause: Possible discoloration pattern resembling examples labelled nutrient deficiency. A photo cannot confirm a nutrient shortage, identify a missing nutrient, or rule out another cause.
actions: Photograph affected and unaffected leaves from the same plant and note their positions.
Record recent watering and fertilizer changes without changing the application rate based on this result.
Ask a local agricultural extension specialist to review the pattern and advise whether testing is needed before adding fertilizer or choosing a treatment.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_sooty_mold
classes.cause: Black fungal film growing on honeydew from aphids, whitefly, scale or mealybug. The mould does not infect the leaf; it blocks light and signals an insect problem.
actions: Find and control the sap-sucking insects underneath -- the mould has no other food source.
Wash heavy deposits off leaves and fruit once the insects are under control.
Watch for ants farming the insects; they will undo the treatment if left alone.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_spider_mite
classes.cause: Spider-mite feeding causes fine stippling, bronzing, and sometimes webbing on leaf undersides.
actions: Confirm moving mites and eggs with a hand lens and map the infested area.
Reduce dust and water stress; conserve or release predatory mites where practical.
Use soap, horticultural oil, or a selective locally approved miticide only when scouting pressure justifies it.

classes.label: Lemon_leaf_yellow_spot
classes.cause: Yellow blotching with several possible causes -- nutrient shortage, mite feeding or early virus symptoms. A single photo cannot separate them.
actions: Check the underside of the leaf with a hand lens for mites before spraying anything.
Compare old and new growth: shortages usually follow a pattern by leaf age.
If the pattern spreads tree to tree, get a laboratory test before treating.
